deck_name: Mastery English - Daily Life Vocabulary Test

content.memory_trigger: Connect “wake up” to one clear daily-life scene.
content.visual_scene: Imagine the action happening in your normal morning or home routine.
content.recall_question: When do you naturally use “wake up” in daily life?

content.example: I usually wake up at 6:30.
People need to wake up to the importance of health.
The company finally woke up to customer complaints.
content.note: Natural when the meaning is extended.

content.example: I usually wake up at 6:30.
The team woke up to the risk too late.
content.note: Useful at work when context fits.

content.example: The screen wakes up when you tap it.
People need to wake up to the importance of health.
content.note: Usually replaced by more formal wording.

content.example: The team woke up to the risk too late.
The team woke up to the risk too late.
I usually wake up at 6:30.

unnatural_zones: Objects or contexts where the action/meaning cannot logically happen
content.short_explanation: Use “wake up” in real daily situations, not as a direct translation for every Tamil idea.

commonly_used: People need to wake up to the importance of health.
The company finally woke up to customer complaints.
not_normally_used: With ideas that do not match the meaning
content.natural_alternative: I wake up in the morning.
content.explanation: The phrase must match the real-life situation and grammar pattern.

content.example: I wake up early.
Please wake me up at 6.
People are waking up to the problem.
I woke up from a strange dream.

sections.name: Paragraph-Based Real-Life Conversation / Story
sections.content: On weekdays, Arun usually wakes up before his alarm, but today he woke up late because he stayed up watching a movie. He checked the time, jumped out of bed, and quickly got ready for work. His mother called from the kitchen, “You finally woke up!” Arun laughed and said he needed stronger coffee today. At the office, he told his colleague, “I woke up late, so I skipped breakfast.” This is how native speakers use wake up naturally in daily life: for the moment sleep ends and the day begins.

content.correct: I wake up in the morning.

content.reason: Wake up means stop sleeping; get out of bed means physically leave the bed.
With pronouns, place the object between wake and up.

content.note: Tamil speakers often mix up wake up and get up.
content.difference: wake up = விழித்துக்கொள்ளுதல்; get up = படுக்கையிலிருந்து எழுந்திருத்தல்.
content.example: I woke up at 6, but I got up at 6:30.

content.example: I need ten minutes to get ready.

content.note: Useful at work when context fits.

content.note: Usually replaced by more formal wording.

content.example: The team is getting ready for the presentation.
The team is getting ready for the presentation.

content.short_explanation: Use “get ready” in real daily situations, not as a direct translation for every Tamil idea.

commonly_used: I need ten minutes to get ready.

not_normally_used: With ideas that do not match the meaning

content.example: I need to get ready.
She is getting ready for work.
We’re getting ready to leave.
Can you get the documents ready?

sections.name: Paragraph-Based Real-Life Conversation / Story
sections.content: It was 8:15, and Meena had only twenty minutes before her bus arrived. She was getting ready for work while her brother was still looking for his keys. Their mother said, “Everyone, get ready quickly. We’re already late.” Meena packed her lunch, checked her phone, and got her bag ready. Before leaving, she said, “I’m ready. Are you coming?” This kind of scene is very natural in English because get ready covers the whole preparation process before leaving, working, studying, or attending an event.

content.reason: Use get ready, not readying, in everyday English.
For objects, use get + object + ready.

content.correct: I get ready for work. / I get ready to go to the office.
content.reason: Use for + noun or to + verb.

content.note: Tamil speakers may translate தயாராகிறேன் directly and say “I am readying.” Natural English is “I’m getting ready.”
content.grammar_trap: Use get ready for + noun, and get ready to + verb.

content.example: We ran out of milk.
I’m running out of time.

content.note: Natural when the meaning is extended.

content.example: We ran out of milk.
We’re running out of budget.
content.note: Useful at work when context fits.

content.example: The device is running out of memory.
I’m running out of time.
content.note: Usually replaced by more formal wording.

content.example: We’re running out of budget.
We’re running out of budget.
We ran out of milk.

unnatural_zones: Objects or contexts where the action/meaning cannot logically happen
content.short_explanation: Use “run out of” in real daily situations, not as a direct translation for every Tamil idea.

commonly_used: She is running out of patience.
not_normally_used: With ideas that do not match the meaning
content.unnatural_example: Milk is finished in my home.
content.explanation: The phrase must match the real-life situation and grammar pattern.

content.example: We ran out of milk.
We’re running out of time.
I’ve almost run out of battery.
She never runs out of ideas.

sections.name: Paragraph-Based Real-Life Conversation / Story
sections.content: On Sunday evening, Kavin opened the fridge and realized they had run out of milk. His phone was also running out of battery, and the grocery store was about to close. He grabbed his wallet, but then noticed he was running out of cash too. So he quickly charged his phone, ordered groceries online, and told his sister, “We need to plan better. We keep running out of basic things.” This story shows how native speakers use run out of naturally for food, battery, money, time, patience, and other limited resources.

content.wrong: Milk is finished in my home.
content.reason: Run out of sounds more natural in daily English.

content.wrong: I am run out of time.
content.correct: I am running out of time.
content.reason: Use am/is/are + running out of for present continuous.

content.correct: My phone is running out of battery. / My battery is dead.
content.reason: Use running out when it is almost empty; dead when fully empty.

content.note: Tamil speakers often say “finished” for everything: milk finished, time finished, battery finished. Natural English often uses run out of.
examples: பால் முடிந்துவிட்டது → We ran out of milk.
நேரம் முடிந்து கொண்டிருக்கிறது → We’re running out of time.
Battery குறைந்து கொண்டிருக்கிறது → My phone is running out of battery.
content.warning: Do not say “I am run out of.” Say “I am running out of.”
